title: Serological and transcriptomic response of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens
abstract: Abstract Bats are hosts to diverse zoonotic viruses which can cause high case fatality rates in humans. Since detecting viruses in bats is difficult, antibodies are often used for surveillance, though their significance remains unclear in the absence of in vivo immunological studies. To address this knowledge gap, we measured antibody production and gene expression in bats following injection with vaccines encoding either a Nipah virus G glycoprotein or an Ebola virus GP glycoprotein. We selected two African bat species with overlapping ranges, Eidolon helvum (confirmed reservoir of henipaviruses) and Epomophorus gambianus (putative reservoir of filoviruses). Using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay and a pseudotype virus neutralization assay, we observed an increase in antibodies against the Nipah glycoprotein in most bats that received the Nipah vaccine. In contrast, we could only detect anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies in one bat species, Ep. gambianus, in response to the Ebola vaccine. Transcriptomic analysis in Ei. helvum revealed that genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Ebola, but not the Nipah, vaccine. These results demonstrate species-specific differences in responses to antigen exposure, offering insights into bat adaptive immune systems and providing calibration for serological data from wild bats.

However, the study is limited by its focus on vaccinated bats rather than natural viral exposure and the use of only two species, which may affect generalizability.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 结果证明了对抗原暴露反应的物种特异性差异,提供了对蝙蝠适应性免疫系统的见解,并为野生蝙蝠的血清学数据提供了校准。

abstract_zh: 摘要 蝙蝠是多种人兽共患病病毒的宿主,这些病毒可导致人类高死亡率。由于在蝙蝠中检测病毒较为困难,抗体常被用于检测,但其意义在缺乏体内免疫学研究的情况下仍不清楚。为了解决这一知识空白,我们测量了蝙蝠在注射表达尼帕病毒G糖蛋白或埃博拉病毒GP糖蛋白的载体后产生的抗体水平和基因表达情况。我们选择了两种在分布范围上有重叠的非洲蝙蝠物种,Eidolon helvum(确认为亨尼帕病毒的宿主)和Epomophorus gambianus(可能为丝状病毒的宿主)。通过基于Luminex的多重微球免疫分析和假型病毒中和试验,我们观察到大多数接受尼帕病毒载体的蝙蝠体内尼帕病毒糖蛋白抗体水平升高。相比之下,我们仅在Ep. gambianus中检测到对埃博拉病毒糖蛋白的抗体反应。在Ei. helvum中进行的转录组分析显示,与埃博拉病毒载体而非尼帕病毒载体反应相关的ISGylation和T细胞分化通路基因存在差异表达。这些结果表明,不同蝙蝠物种对抗原暴露的反应存在特异性差异,为了解蝙蝠适应性免疫系统提供了见解,并为野外蝙蝠的血清学数据校准提供了框架。

title: CRISPR/Cas13a-Based Nucleic Acid-Functionalized Discrete Floating-Gate Field-Effect Transistor for Amplification-Free Rapid Nipah Virus Detection
abstract: Abstract Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal zoonotic pathogen, and existing rapid diagnostic tools are scarce and reliant on nucleic acid amplification. In this study, we designed and fabricated a thin-film field-effect transistor with an IGZO channel and, for the first time, combined a discrete AuNP floating gate with the CRISPR/Cas13a system to achieve amplification-free detection of NiV. A pair of partially complementary nucleic acid reporter probes was used to attach AuNPs onto the channel, forming a nucleic acid-functionalized discrete floating gate. Under positive gate voltage, the AuNPs electrostatically induce mirror charges in the IGZO channel, amplifying the sensing signal. Additionally, the electrons can be injected from AuNPs into the channel via the Fowler–Nordheim tunneling effect under negative gate voltage, as a potential complementary sensing mechanism. The AuNPs are immobilized via nucleic acid strands, ensuring good biocompatibility. CrRNA was designed and the CRISPR system was optimized for compatibility with the FET, achieving amplification-free detection of NiV standards down to 10° copies/μL within 10 min. This study not only provides a reliable and rapid detection tool for NiV but also establishes a biosensing framework applicable to other pathogens.

abstract_zh: 摘要 尼帕病毒(尼帕病毒)是一种高致死率的人兽共患病病原体,现有的快速诊断工具稀缺且依赖于核酸扩增。在本研究中,我们设计并制造了一种具有IGZO沟道的薄膜场效应晶体管,并首次将离散的金纳米颗粒(AuNPs)浮动栅与CRISPR/Cas13a系统结合,实现了对尼帕病毒的无扩增检测。通过一对部分互补的核酸报告探针将AuNPs固定在沟道上,形成核酸功能化的离散浮动栅。在正栅压下,AuNPs静电感应IGZO沟道中的镜像电荷,从而放大传感信号。此外,在负栅压下,AuNPs可通过费尔德-诺德海姆隧穿效应将电子注入沟道,作为潜在的互补传感机制。AuNPs通过核酸链固定,确保良好的生物相容性。设计了CrRNA并优化了CRISPR系统以适配场效应晶体管,实现了在10分钟内对尼帕病毒标准品的无扩增检测,灵敏度达到10° copies/μL。本研究不仅为尼帕病毒提供了一种可靠且快速的检测工具,还建立了一种适用于其他病原体的生物传感框架。

title: Absence of Nipah virus antibodies and detection of Porcine kobuvirus, Porcine enterovirus-9 and Bocavirus in pigs during a Nipah virus outbreak investigation in West Bengal, India
abstract: The Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal zoonotic virus that causes respiratory disease and encephalitis in humans. Historically, the NiV outbreaks in Malaysia and Singapore (1998–1999) involved domestic pigs as amplifying intermediate hosts, whereas subsequent outbreaks in India and Bangladesh have primarily been attributed to direct bat-to-human transmission or nosocomial spread, with no documented involvement of livestock. The role of intermediate hosts in NiV transmission is less studied. We report findings from a study conducted in West Bengal during the NiV outbreak in January 2026, investigating the role of local pig populations in NiV transmission and screening diseased pigs for other etiologies using metagenomic sequencing. Blood, nasal, rectal, throat and ocular swab samples were collected from 119 domestic pigs in Nadia, Kolkata, North 24 Paraganas, and Purba Bardhaman districts of West Bengal. Virological and serological tests for NiV infection were performed using real-time qRT-PCR and swine IgG ELISA. A subset of nasal and rectal swab samples from diseased pigs also underwent metagenomic sequencing. All swab samples tested negative for NiV RNA, and no antibodies were found in the serum samples. Metagenomic sequencing detected genomes of Porcine Kobuvirus (PKV) and Porcine enterovirus 9 (PEV9), prevalent in the Indian pig population as well as Porcine Bocavirus (PBoV), adding to the limited molecular reports of PBoV from India. The serological and virological investigation conducted in 119 pigs from West Bengal revealed no evidence of NiV infection. The detection of other prevalent porcine viruses and PBoV, a relatively infrequently reported virus from India, emphasizes the need for genomic surveillance and incorporation of the One Health concept into disease surveillance.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查在印度西孟加拉邦尼帕病毒暴发期间,当地猪群在尼帕病毒传播中的作用,并筛查其他潜在病因。尼帕病毒(尼帕病毒)是一种高致死性的动物源性病毒,可引起人类呼吸道疾病和脑炎。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究在印度西孟加拉邦尼帕病毒暴发期间进行,时间为2026年1月,重点调查了来自纳迪亚、加尔各答、北24区和东巴尔杜曼地区的119头家猪。该调查旨在确定猪是否参与了尼帕病毒的传播,并筛查其他病毒。
elements_zh.methods: 使用实时qRT-PCR和猪IgG ELISA对尼帕病毒感染进行了病毒学和血清学检测。此外,部分患病猪的鼻腔和直肠拭子样本也进行了宏基因组测序,以检测其他病毒。
elements_zh.main_results: 所有拭子样本均未检测到尼帕病毒RNA,血清样本中也未发现抗体。宏基因组测序检测到了猪 kobuvirus(PKV)和猪肠病毒9(PEV9)的病毒序列,这些病毒在印度猪群中普遍存在,同时还检测到了猪博卡病毒(PBoV),该病毒在印度的报道相对较少。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,在此次暴发期间,猪并未参与尼帕病毒的传播,并突显了该地区存在其他猪病毒。这为印度的PBoV分子报告提供了补充。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果强调了对基因组监测的必要性,并突出了将‘一个健康’概念纳入疾病监测的重要性,特别是在监测像尼帕病毒这样的新兴病原体时。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于一次暴发调查,未包括长期监测或更广泛的生态数据。尼帕病毒缺失的证据较强,但其他病毒的检测可能未能完全解释尼帕病毒的传播动态。

We report findings from a study conducted in West Bengal during the NiV outbreak in January 2026, investigating the role of local pig populations in NiV transmission and screening diseased pigs for other etiologies using metagenomic sequencing. Blood, nasal, rectal, throat and ocular swab samples were collected from 119 domestic pigs in Nadia, Kolkata, North 24 Paraganas, and Purba Bardhaman districts of West Bengal. Virological and serological tests for NiV infection were performed using real-time qRT-PCR and swine IgG ELISA. A subset of nasal and rectal swab samples from diseased pigs also underwent metagenomic sequencing. All swab samples tested negative for NiV RNA, and no antibodies were found in the serum samples. Metagenomic sequencing detected genomes of Porcine Kobuvirus (PKV) and Porcine enterovirus 9 (PEV9), prevalent in the Indian pig population as well as Porcine Bocavirus (PBoV), adding to the limited molecular reports of PBoV from India. The serological and virological investigation conducted in 119 pigs from West Bengal revealed no evidence of NiV infection. The detection of other prevalent porcine viruses and PBoV, a relatively infrequently reported virus from India, emphasizes the need for genomic surveillance and incorporation of the One Health concept into disease surveillance.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在调查在印度西孟加拉邦尼帕病毒暴发期间,当地猪群在尼帕病毒传播中的作用,并筛查其他潜在病因。尼帕病毒(尼帕病毒)是一种高致死性的动物源性病毒,可引起人类呼吸道疾病和脑炎。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究在印度西孟加拉邦尼帕病毒暴发期间进行,时间为2026年1月,重点调查了来自纳迪亚、加尔各答、北24区和东巴尔杜曼地区的119头家猪。该调查旨在确定猪是否参与了尼帕病毒的传播,并筛查其他病毒。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用实时qRT-PCR和猪IgG ELISA对尼帕病毒感染进行了病毒学和血清学检测。此外,部分患病猪的鼻腔和直肠拭子样本也进行了宏基因组测序,以检测其他病毒。
analysis_zh.main_results: 所有拭子样本均未检测到尼帕病毒RNA,血清样本中也未发现抗体。宏基因组测序检测到了猪 kobuvirus(PKV)和猪肠病毒9(PEV9)的病毒序列,这些病毒在印度猪群中普遍存在,同时还检测到了猪博卡病毒(PBoV),该病毒在印度的报道相对较少。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,在此次暴发期间,猪并未参与尼帕病毒的传播,并突显了该地区存在其他猪病毒。这为印度的PBoV分子报告提供了补充。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果强调了对基因组监测的必要性,并突出了将‘一个健康’概念纳入疾病监测的重要性,特别是在监测像尼帕病毒这样的新兴病原体时。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于一次暴发调查,未包括长期监测或更广泛的生态数据。尼帕病毒缺失的证据较强,但其他病毒的检测可能未能完全解释尼帕病毒的传播动态。

title: A dual-glycoprotein-targeting bispecific nanoantibody confers potent neutralization against Nipah virus.
abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a biosafety level 4 pathogen that has consistently posed a significant threat to public health. The two envelope proteins on the viral surface, the receptor-binding protein (RBP) and the fusion (F) protein, are the primary targets of neutralizing antibodies. However, the use of antibodies targeting a single viral antigen often leads to the emergence of resistant strains. abstract_zh: 尼帕病毒(NiV)是一种生物安全等级4的病原体,一直对公共卫生构成重大威胁。病毒表面的两种包膜蛋白,受体结合蛋白(RBP)和融合(F)蛋白,是中和抗体的主要靶标。然而,针对单一病毒抗原的抗体常导致耐药株的出现。在此研究中,通过噬菌体展示库筛选,我们获得了一种C型纳米抗体(C-Nab),G-3-1,其靶向RBP的头部结构域。半衰期延长的G-3-1-HLE有效保护仓鼠免受真实NiV的挑战。此外,我们通过刚性(AP)12连接子将G-3-1与靶向F蛋白的纳米抗体2A1-3-8连接,构建了融合蛋白2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1。该融合蛋白表现出增强且平衡的中和活性。此外,在NiV假病毒感染的小鼠模型中验证了2A1-3-8-(AP)12-G-3-1的体内预防效果。总体而言,这项针对双包膜蛋白靶向的双特异性抗体的研究不仅提供了一种有前景的抗病毒药物候选药物,还为下一代抗体优化提供了重要的设计策略。

title: Emerging respiratory infectious diseases: Clinical aspects for rapid identification and management.
abstract: Emerging respiratory infectious diseases increasingly arise at the human-animal-environment interface and challenge clinicians with rapidly evolving diagnostic, therapeutic, and infection-control decisions. This narrative review summarizes clinically relevant viral and bacterial pathogens that may present as severe respiratory disease, but are easily mistaken for common community-acquired infections during early illness. We focus on zoonotic influenza A viruses, including contemporary H5N1, Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), hantaviruses, Nipah virus, and inhalational bacterial threats such as anthrax, pneumonic plague, tularemia, and melioidosis. These infections may progress from non-specific symptoms to severe pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, shock, neurological complications, disseminated infection, or death. Timely recognition depends on careful assessment of travel, occupational and recreational exposures, animal contact, outbreak signals, and pathogen-specific syndromic clues. Multiplex molecular diagnostics can support early triage and exclusion of common pathogens, but targeted PCR, culture, serology, sequencing, and reference laboratory confirmation remain essential. Management requires prompt supportive care, appropriate isolation, public health notification, and pathogen-directed antimicrobial, antiviral, antitoxin, or prophylactic strategies where available. By integrating clinical presentation, diagnostics, treatment, vaccines, and One Health considerations, this review aims to translate knowledge on emerging infections into practical bedside preparedness.

abstract_zh: 新兴呼吸道传染病越来越多地出现在人类-动物-环境的交界处,给临床医生带来快速演变的诊断、治疗和感染控制决策的挑战。本叙述性综述总结了可能表现为严重呼吸道疾病但早期病程中容易被误诊为常见社区获得性感染的临床相关病毒和细菌病原体。我们重点讨论了人兽共患的流感A病毒,包括当前的H5N1、中东呼吸综合征冠状病毒(MERS-CoV)、汉坦病毒、尼帕病毒以及吸入性细菌威胁如炭疽、肺炎鼠疫、兔热病和类鼻疽。这些感染可能从非特异性症状发展为严重肺炎、急性呼吸窘迫综合征、休克、神经系统并发症、播散性感染或死亡。及时识别依赖于对旅行、职业和休闲暴露、动物接触、暴发信号以及病原体特异性综合征线索的细致评估。多重分子诊断可支持早期分诊和排除常见病原体,但靶向PCR、培养、血清学、测序和参考实验室确认仍然是关键。管理需要及时的支持性治疗、适当的隔离、公共卫生通报以及在可获得的情况下针对病原体的抗菌、抗病毒药物、抗毒素或预防性策略。通过整合临床表现、诊断、治疗、疫苗以及One Health考虑因素,本综述旨在将关于新兴感染的知识转化为临床床边的实用准备能力。

title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses
abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses.
analysis.methods: SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically.
analysis.main_results: In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: However, the study does not report on the long-term effects of SLR14 treatment and the generalizability of the findings to other host species remains to be determined.

analysis.summary_en: The study evaluated the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an RIG-I agonist, against a range of highly pathogenic viruses, including Ebola, Marburg, and Nipah viruses. SLR14 provided broad-spectrum protection, reducing viral replication and improving survival rates in both in vitro and in vivo models. The findings suggest SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with potential for use against lethal viral pathogens.

title_zh: 免疫调节RIG-I激动剂SLR14对多种高致病性负链RNA病毒具有保护作用
source_body_en: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

title: Epitope and immunological basis for superior immunogenicity of henipavirus glycoprotein HeV.G over NiV.G in mRNA vaccines
abstract: Nipah (NiV) and Hendra (HeV) viruses are highly lethal zoonotic Henipaviruses with pandemic potential, for which no licensed vaccines exist. The surface glycoprotein (G) is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet a systematic comparison of the immunogenicity of NiV.G and HeV.G has been lacking. Here, we engineered mRNA vaccines encoding the full-length G proteins of NiV and HeV. In Syrian hamsters, while both vaccines conferred homologous protection, only HeV.G vaccination at a lower dose (5 μg) provided complete cross-protection against lethal NiV challenge. Comparative immune profiling revealed that HeV.G vaccination induced significantly higher neutralizing antibody titers, which correlated with robust germinal center B cell expansion and a stronger CD4 + T follicular helper (Tfh) cell response, despite equivalent B cell activation. Epitope mapping uncovered a structurally conserved yet immunologically divergent MHC class II-restricted peptide (YIAITKVER) in HeV.G with superior predicted binding affinity, providing a mechanistic basis for the enhanced T cell help. Our work establishes HeV.G as a superior vaccine immunogen due to its distinct epitope repertoire and underscores the critical role of CD4 + T cell help in driving cross-protective B cell immunity. We further developed a bivalent vaccine Gmix, which induced balanced antibody and cellular immune responses against both G proteins, thereby confirming the value of multivalent vaccines in broadening immune coverage. Collectively, this study defines HeV.G as the preferred antigen for pan-henipavirus vaccine development and offers a framework for rational antigen selection against future viral threats.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the immunogenicity of the glycoprotein (G) from Nipah virus (NiV) and Hendra virus (HeV) in mRNA vaccines. It highlights the lack of systematic comparison between NiV.G and HeV.G, despite their shared status as highly lethal zoonotic Henipaviruses. The research engineered mRNA vaccines encoding the full-length G proteins of both viruses and evaluated their protective efficacy in Syrian hamsters. Results showed that HeV.G vaccination at a lower dose (5 μg) provided complete cross-protection against lethal NiV challenge, while both vaccines offered homologous protection. Immune profiling revealed that HeV.G induced significantly higher neutralizing antibody titers, associated with robust B cell expansion and a stronger CD4+ T follicular helper (Tfh) cell response, despite equivalent B cell activation. Epitope mapping identified a structurally conserved yet immunologically divergent MHC class II-restricted peptide in HeV.G with superior predicted binding affinity, explaining the enhanced T cell help. The study concludes that HeV.G is a superior vaccine immunogen for pan-henipavirus development, emphasizing the role of CD4+ T cell help in cross-protective immunity. It also suggests the potential of multivalent vaccines in broadening immune coverage. The findings do not report specific limitations, but the evidence is strong due to the direct comparison of immunogenicity and mechanistic insights.

title: Serological and transcriptomic response of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens

source_records.title: Serological and transcriptomic response of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens

full_text: AbstractBats are hosts to diverse zoonotic viruses which can cause high case fatality rates in humans. Since detecting viruses in bats is difficult, antibodies are often used for surveillance, though their significance remains unclear in the absence of in vivo immunological studies. To address this knowledge gap, we measured antibody production and gene expression in bats following injection with vaccines encoding either a Nipah virus G glycoprotein or an Ebola virus GP glycoprotein. We selected two African bat species with overlapping ranges, Eidolon helvum (confirmed reservoir of henipaviruses) and Epomophorus gambianus (putative reservoir of filoviruses). Using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay and a pseudotype virus neutralization assay, we observed an increase in antibodies against the Nipah glycoprotein in most bats that received the Nipah vaccine. In contrast, we could only detect anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies in one bat species, Ep. gambianus, in response to the Ebola vaccine. Transcriptomic analysis in Ei. helvum revealed that genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Ebola, but not the Nipah, vaccine. These results demonstrate species-specific differences in responses to antigen exposure, offering insights into bat adaptive immune systems and providing calibration for serological data from wild bats.Keywords: Eidolon helvum, Epomophorus gambianus, henipavirus, Paramyxoviridae, Filoviridae, gene expression, antibody production 5.Material and methods5.1.Facility and animalsWild bats were caught at their roosts in Accra, Ghana, in June 2017, using mist nets. We targeted two species of fruit bat, the African straw-coloured fruit bat Ei. helvum and the Gambian epauletted fruit bat Ep. gambianus. Any juvenile or adult female bats captured were released immediately, while adult males were placed in individual canvas bags and transported by road to the nearby purpose-built experimental facilities maintained by the Wildlife Division of the Government of Ghana in Achimota Forest, Accra. A total of 75 bats were captured over three consecutive nights. We only kept adult males (27 Ei. helvum and 33 Ep. gambianus) to reduce physiological variability owing to age or pregnancy status, and the number of animals was constrained by logistical and ethical factors. After an initial observation period to exclude unhealthy or aggressive bats, 19 Ei. helvum and 14 Ep. gambianus bats were individually tagged with intradermal microchips and were placed in smaller cages (80 × 80 × 80 cm) in single-species groups of up to five bats for the rest of the study (two months). These cages were suspended from the roof of the animal house and separated by approximately 2 m of space and tin baffles to prevent direct physical contact between bats and indirect contact via droplets (urine, secretions, food and water). Bats received diced mixed fruits (e.g. mango, papaya and banana) and ad libitum water, which were replaced every day [87]. Bats were monitored by veterinarians for 8–10 days before the start of the experiment. During the experiment, bats were regularly assessed by veterinarians for signs of distress, weight loss or injury. If the welfare of any bat was seriously reduced, it was euthanized on humane grounds. Unexpectedly, Epomophorus bats did not cope well with captivity and either died suddenly or had to be euthanized on the basis of weight loss: four survived until the second injection and only three completed the whole two-month study (figure 1).5.2.VaccinesFour live recombinant viral vaccines were produced by the Viral Vector Core Facility (University of Oxford) for the purpose of this study. Two were recombinant chimpanzee adenovirus (ChAdOx1), one of which encoded the Zaire ebola virus (Orthoebolavirus zairense Makona strain) GP protein and the other a Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense Bangladesh strain) G protein. The other two vaccines were MVA, one encoding the same Zaire ebolavirus Makona G protein and the other with no added genes following unsuccessful attempts to insert the Nipah virus G protein into the MVA. This heterologous ‘prime-boost’ vaccination strategy (adenovirus vector followed by boosting with MVA vector) was previously validated in clinical trials of Ebola vaccines [47] and in animal experiments against diverse pathogens [88,89]. The presence of the antigen in each vaccine was confirmed by ID PCR. For each vaccine, the recombinant virus was titrated and assayed by spectrophotometry to measure the number of virus particles ml−1. The sterility of the virus was confirmed by inoculation of TSB broth with 10 μl of purified virus and incubation for 3 days at 35°C. See results of quality control in the supplementary material (viral vectors). The vaccines were shipped on dry ice to the University of Ghana, and the cold chain was maintained until the vaccines were used.5.3.Experimental designBats of each species were arbitrarily split into three groups for injections with the Ebola vaccines, the Nipah vaccines or PBS, respectively. Given a maximum capacity of 50 bats in the facilities, the original study design aimed for 25 bats from each species, to be housed in groups of five. Owing to premature release or euthanasia of captured bats on welfare grounds during the initial observation period, only 19 Ei. helvum (nEbola = 8, nNipah = 7, nPBS = 4) and 14 Ep. gambianus (nEbola = 6, nNipah = 5, nPBS = 3) were eventually enrolled in the study. An initial blood sample of 0.5 ml was collected from each enrolled bat prior to vaccine exposure. Bats were first injected with either the ChAdOx1 vaccine (dosed to ca 107 IU) or PBS intramuscularly (volume 0.25 ml) and four weeks later with either the MVA vaccine (dosed to ca 107 pfu) or PBS. Blood samples of 0.3 ml were collected from the propatagial vein of each bat weekly for up to eight weeks, starting on the day of the first injection (in Eidolon) and the day after the first injection (in Epomophorus). Finally, on week 8 after the initial injection, all bats were euthanized by overdose of intravenous ketamine/medetomidine, then exsanguinated, and samples from a range of organs (brain, liver, spleen, kidney and where possible lymph node) were harvested. Every blood sample was immediately split into two aliquots, to one of which an RNA preservative (RNAlater) was added to stabilize the RNA. Organ samples were preserved with the same RNA preservative. Stabilized whole blood, remaining whole blood and organ samples were transported on ice to the Biochemistry Department (University of Ghana). The whole blood aliquot (without RNAlater) was centrifuged, and serum was split between two tubes. Serum samples were heat-treated at 56°C for 30 min to inactivate any pathogens. All samples were stored at −80°C at the University of Ghana, and one serum aliquot as well as organ samples were shipped to the Institute of Zoology in London in a liquid nitrogen dry shipper for analysis, in accordance with export and import permits delivered by Ghana and UK government agencies, respectively.5.4.Serology5.4.1.Multiplex microsphere-based immunoassayWe used a Luminex xMAP–based multiplex MIA to measure antigen-specific antibody binding, recorded as MFI units [48–51]. The Bio-Plex LX100/200, RRID:SCR_018025 (Luminex Corporation, Austin, TX) was used to measure the relative levels of bat serum antibodies against a panel of eight recombinant viral glycoprotein antigens (from three henipaviruses and two filoviruses): Cedar virus F and G proteins, Hendra virus F and G proteins, Nipah virus F and G proteins, Ebola virus GP protein (NC_002549.1) and Marburg virus GP protein, produced as native-like, soluble, oligomeric trimers (F and GP) or tetramers (G) [49,50,90,91]. As positive controls, serial dilutions of four monoclonal antibodies (5D2 against Ebola virus glycoprotein, 2B8 against Marburg virus, 102.4 against Hendra/Nipah G protein and 14F3 against Cedar virus) were tested against the same panel of antigens alongside bat serum samples (supplementary material, figure S1). As negative controls, two wells per plate were filled with the same reagents but no serum (supplementary material, figure S19). MFI values from Ei. helvum serum samples against the Nipah virus G protein were previously shown to correlate with neutralization assay titration against Hendra virus and Nipah virus [53] and have been used in several studies to monitor seroprevalence and infer virus circulation in Ei. helvum bat populations (e.g. [70,92]). Peel et al. [53] suggested 500 MFI as a cut-off point for Nipah virus G protein assay to maximize sensitivity based on receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve analysis against neutralization data using serum from wild Ei. helvum. To date, we are not aware of similar validation data for other antigens or other bat species.A total of 413 serum samples were tested by MIA in duplicate against the panel of eight antigens alongside negative controls. Of these, 13 readings failed and 12 samples had to be discarded after quality control as they yielded fewer than 100 microspheres. After log10 transformation of the MFI values, we flagged a small number of samples with duplicate variation above 0.5 units but did not exclude them. Here we focus on the MIA data for the Nipah G and Ebola G antigens as these matched the vaccine antigens; other antibodies showed very little temporal variations (figure 3B and supplementary material, figure S2). Because of the low number of Ep. gambianus bats that could be tested, we did not carry out any statistical tests on the data from this species.5.4.2.Pseudotyped virus production and neutralization assaysTwo sets of pseudotyped virus were generated using a three-plasmid, second-generation lentiviral system as previously described [93,94]. The first set carried filovirus glycoproteins (GP) from, respectively, Ebola virus (EBOV) Mayinga (EU224440), EBOV Makona (KJ660346.2), Sudan virus (SUDV; FJ968794), Lloviu cuevavirus (LLOV; JF828358), Marburg virus (MARV) Kenya (Z12132) and MARV DRC (DQ447650). A second set carried the fusion (F) and attachment (G) glycoproteins from, respectively, Nipah virus Malaysia (NIVm; AF212302), Nipah virus Bangladesh (NIVb; JN808864.1) and the Ghana virus M74a (HQ660129). Henipavirus and filovirus pseudotyped virus neutralizing titres were determined using endpoint 50% tissue culture infectious dose (TCID50) assays [95] on human embryonic kidney 293T clone-17 (HEK 293T/17; American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), CRL-11268) and Chinese hamster ovary K1 (CHO-K1; ATCC, CCL-61), respectively. HEK293T/17 were cultured in a humidified, 37°C, 5% CO2 incubator with high glucose Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium (DMEM; Merck) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Merck). CHO-K1 cells were cultured in the same conditions using Ham's F-12 nutrient mix (Merck) plus 10% FBS.A serial dilution (3-fold dilutions; 1 : 50–1 : 12 150) of the bat serum samples was set up in a white 96-well plate (Thermo Fisher), before 100 × TCID50 of the specific PV was added. These were incubated for 1 h at 37°C before 2 × 104 of the necessary cells (HEK293T/17 for NIVb and M74a; CHO-K1 for EBOV, SUDV, LLOV and MARV) were added and the plates returned to the incubator for a further 48 h. After this the supernatant was removed and a 50 : 50 mix of Bright-Glo (Promega) and serum-free media added to each well. The luciferase activity was measured in relative light units and neutralizing activity determined using the virus samples that were incubated with a non-specific serum that was negative for antibodies targeting our viral entry protein (VEP) of interest.5.5.RNA sequencing in Eidolon helvum5.5.1.Sample selectionWe selected whole blood samples from a subset of Ei. helvum individuals (Ebola vaccine group n = 8, Nipah vaccine group n = 3, PBS group n = 2; supplementary material, table S1) for transcriptome analysis. We excluded Ep. gambianus because of the low number of bats. For logistical reasons, the samples were selected, processed for RNA extraction and sent for sequencing before the serology results were known. One bat from the PBS-injected group was then revealed to have high antibody response against the Nipah G protein in the MIA before the start of the experiment (figure 2 and supplementary material, figure S5) and was, therefore, excluded from the differential expression analysis, thus leaving one individual as a negative control for the differential expression analysis. As the Nipah vaccine group received an empty vaccine vector as a booster (in contrast to the Ebola vaccine group), gene expression analysis was conducted only up to four weeks post prime vaccine exposure to enable meaningful comparisons between the groups.5.5.2.RNA extraction and sequencingRNA was isolated from 150 μl whole blood using the RNAzol® BD kit (Molecular Research Centre, Inc.), following the large RNA isolation protocol with volumes of reagents reduced as follows to account for the small input volume: 300 μl RNAzol® BD, 4.05 μl acetic acid, 450 μl lysate, 22.5 μl 1-bromo-3-chloropropane (BCP), 78.75 μl isopropanol, 60–120 μl 75% ethanol. In step 4, 225 μl supernatant was used. RNA was quantified using a NanoDrop 2000 (Thermo Fisher), and RNA integrity was determined using a 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). Samples were paired-end-sequenced by Novogene, UK with 150 bp read length on an Illumina sequencer (Illumina, USA). The average number of raw sequencing reads per sample was 26.25 ± 3.02 Mb (mean ± s.d. PE150).5.5.3.Quality check and read mappingThe quality of the RNA sequencing data was evaluated using the FastQC software v. 0.11.4 [96], and low-quality sequences were trimmed using the bbduk.sh script from the BBTools bioinformatics package (https://sourceforge.net/projects/bbmap/). First, over-represented sequences as detected during the quality check and adaptor sequences (ref = adapters.fa.gz) were removed. Approximately 75% of the transcripts from the blood samples mapped to haemoglobin and were thus removed from the dataset. Further, the leftmost 10 bases of the sequencing reads (ftl = 10), and both ends (qtrim = rl) were trimmed until the average read quality (Phred score) was 10 or greater (trimq = 10). Finally, any reads shorter than 25 bp (minlen = 25) were discarded. After removal of over-represented sequences and trimming, an average of 6.82 ± 3.08 Mb sequencing reads remained for the blood samples. The quality filtered reads from each blood sample were then aligned to an in-house-generated Ei. helvum draft genome assembly and annotation file (available on figshare [57]) and the gene expression level quantified using STAR v. 2.7.3a with default options and –quantMode GeneCounts [97]. The percentage of trimmed sequencing reads that mapped to a unique location in the Ei. helvum genome ranged from 76 to 88%.Owing to low-quality RNA from the PBS-injected bat taken at two weeks post injection, no comparison was made between the PBS- and vaccine-injected (treatment) groups at two weeks post prime injection. The differential expression analysis was thus conducted using data from one PBS-injected individual, two or three Nipah vaccine-treated bats and six to eight Ebola vaccine-treated bats depending on the time point (figure 5A and supplementary material, table S1).5.5.4.Principal component analysisA principal component analysis (PCA) was used to visualize sample-to-sample distances solely on the basis of their gene expression profiles using the plotPCA function in DESeq2 v. 1.36.0 [98] in R v. 4.2.1 [99]. One control individual with high anti-Hendra virus antibody levels (supplementary material, figure S5) clustered as an outlier in the PCA (supplementary material, figure S20) and was, therefore, excluded from the differential expression analysis, leaving a single PBS individual for all comparisons. A temporal pattern was observed in the transcriptomic data (supplementary material, figure S20), which was controlled for by comparing PBS-injected and vaccine-treated groups for each time point separately.5.5.5.Differential gene expression analysisTo investigate which genes were up- or down-regulated in response to each vaccine, gene expression levels between the PBS group and each vaccine-treated group were compared in blood samples at each time point (one to four weeks post prime vaccine exposure). To identify genes that were differentially expressed between the Nipah and the Ebola vaccine group, gene expression levels were further compared between each vaccine group in blood samples from one to four weeks post prime vaccine exposure. All differential gene expression analyses were conducted in DESeq2 v. 1.36.0 [98], which takes the low number of replicates into account [100]. p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini and Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple testing [101]. Genes with an FDR less than 0.05 were considered differentially expressed.The top DEGs from each time point for each vaccine group were identified, and their fold change visualized in heat maps using the pheatmap package [102]. Upset plots [103] were then used to explore whether the same genes were differentially expressed at different time points. The results from the differential expression analysis between the Nipah and the Ebola vaccine group were visualized in volcano plots using the R package EnhancedVolcano v. 1.14.0 [104]. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractBats are hosts to diverse zoonotic viruses which can cause high case fatality rates in humans. Since detecting viruses in bats is difficult, antibodies are often used for surveillance, though their significance remains unclear in the absence of in vivo immunological studies. To address this knowledge gap, we measured antibody production and gene expression in bats following injection with vaccines encoding either a Nipah virus G glycoprotein or an Ebola virus GP glycoprotein. We selected two African bat species with overlapping ranges, Eidolon helvum (confirmed reservoir of henipaviruses) and Epomophorus gambianus (putative reservoir of filoviruses). Using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay and a pseudotype virus neutralization assay, we observed an increase in antibodies against the Nipah glycoprotein in most bats that received the Nipah vaccine. In contrast, we could only detect anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies in one bat species, Ep. gambianus, in response to the Ebola vaccine. Transcriptomic analysis in Ei. helvum revealed that genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Ebola, but not the Nipah, vaccine. These results demonstrate species-specific differences in responses to antigen exposure, offering insights into bat adaptive immune systems and providing calibration for serological data from wild bats.Keywords: Eidolon helvum, Epomophorus gambianus, henipavirus, Paramyxoviridae, Filoviridae, gene expression, antibody production
full_text_sections.methods: 5.Material and methods5.1.Facility and animalsWild bats were caught at their roosts in Accra, Ghana, in June 2017, using mist nets. We targeted two species of fruit bat, the African straw-coloured fruit bat Ei. helvum and the Gambian epauletted fruit bat Ep. gambianus. Any juvenile or adult female bats captured were released immediately, while adult males were placed in individual canvas bags and transported by road to the nearby purpose-built experimental facilities maintained by the Wildlife Division of the Government of Ghana in Achimota Forest, Accra. A total of 75 bats were captured over three consecutive nights. We only kept adult males (27 Ei. helvum and 33 Ep. gambianus) to reduce physiological variability owing to age or pregnancy status, and the number of animals was constrained by logistical and ethical factors. After an initial observation period to exclude unhealthy or aggressive bats, 19 Ei. helvum and 14 Ep. gambianus bats were individually tagged with intradermal microchips and were placed in smaller cages (80 × 80 × 80 cm) in single-species groups of up to five bats for the rest of the study (two months). These cages were suspended from the roof of the animal house and separated by approximately 2 m of space and tin baffles to prevent direct physical contact between bats and indirect contact via droplets (urine, secretions, food and water). Bats received diced mixed fruits (e.g. mango, papaya and banana) and ad libitum water, which were replaced every day [87]. Bats were monitored by veterinarians for 8–10 days before the start of the experiment. During the experiment, bats were regularly assessed by veterinarians for signs of distress, weight loss or injury. If the welfare of any bat was seriously reduced, it was euthanized on humane grounds. Unexpectedly, Epomophorus bats did not cope well with captivity and either died suddenly or had to be euthanized on the basis of weight loss: four survived until the second injection and only three completed the whole two-month study (figure 1).5.2.VaccinesFour live recombinant viral vaccines were produced by the Viral Vector Core Facility (University of Oxford) for the purpose of this study. Two were recombinant chimpanzee adenovirus (ChAdOx1), one of which encoded the Zaire ebola virus (Orthoebolavirus zairense Makona strain) GP protein and the other a Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense Bangladesh strain) G protein. The other two vaccines were MVA, one encoding the same Zaire ebolavirus Makona G protein and the other with no added genes following unsuccessful attempts to insert the Nipah virus G protein into the MVA. This heterologous ‘prime-boost’ vaccination strategy (adenovirus vector followed by boosting with MVA vector) was previously validated in clinical trials of Ebola vaccines [47] and in animal experiments against diverse pathogens [88,89]. The presence of the antigen in each vaccine was confirmed by ID PCR. For each vaccine, the recombinant virus was titrated and assayed by spectrophotometry to measure the number of virus particles ml−1. The sterility of the virus was confirmed by inoculation of TSB broth with 10 μl of purified virus and incubation for 3 days at 35°C. See results of quality control in the supplementary material (viral vectors). The vaccines were shipped on dry ice to the University of Ghana, and the cold chain was maintained until the vaccines were used.5.3.Experimental designBats of each species were arbitrarily split into three groups for injections with the Ebola vaccines, the Nipah vaccines or PBS, respectively. Given a maximum capacity of 50 bats in the facilities, the original study design aimed for 25 bats from each species, to be housed in groups of five. Owing to premature release or euthanasia of captured bats on welfare grounds during the initial observation period, only 19 Ei. helvum (nEbola = 8, nNipah = 7, nPBS = 4) and 14 Ep. gambianus (nEbola = 6, nNipah = 5, nPBS = 3) were eventually enrolled in the study. An initial blood sample of 0.5 ml was collected from each enrolled bat prior to vaccine exposure. Bats were first injected with either the ChAdOx1 vaccine (dosed to ca 107 IU) or PBS intramuscularly (volume 0.25 ml) and four weeks later with either the MVA vaccine (dosed to ca 107 pfu) or PBS. Blood samples of 0.3 ml were collected from the propatagial vein of each bat weekly for up to eight weeks, starting on the day of the first injection (in Eidolon) and the day after the first injection (in Epomophorus). Finally, on week 8 after the initial injection, all bats were euthanized by overdose of intravenous ketamine/medetomidine, then exsanguinated, and samples from a range of organs (brain, liver, spleen, kidney and where possible lymph node) were harvested. Every blood sample was immediately split into two aliquots, to one of which an RNA preservative (RNAlater) was added to stabilize the RNA. Organ samples were preserved with the same RNA preservative. Stabilized whole blood, remaining whole blood and organ samples were transported on ice to the Biochemistry Department (University of Ghana). The whole blood aliquot (without RNAlater) was centrifuged, and serum was split between two tubes. Serum samples were heat-treated at 56°C for 30 min to inactivate any pathogens. All samples were stored at −80°C at the University of Ghana, and one serum aliquot as well as organ samples were shipped to the Institute of Zoology in London in a liquid nitrogen dry shipper for analysis, in accordance with export and import permits delivered by Ghana and UK government agencies, respectively.5.4.Serology5.4.1.Multiplex microsphere-based immunoassayWe used a Luminex xMAP–based multiplex MIA to measure antigen-specific antibody binding, recorded as MFI units [48–51]. The Bio-Plex LX100/200, RRID:SCR_018025 (Luminex Corporation, Austin, TX) was used to measure the relative levels of bat serum antibodies against a panel of eight recombinant viral glycoprotein antigens (from three henipaviruses and two filoviruses): Cedar virus F and G proteins, Hendra virus F and G proteins, Nipah virus F and G proteins, Ebola virus GP protein (NC_002549.1) and Marburg virus GP protein, produced as native-like, soluble, oligomeric trimers (F and GP) or tetramers (G) [49,50,90,91]. As positive controls, serial dilutions of four monoclonal antibodies (5D2 against Ebola virus glycoprotein, 2B8 against Marburg virus, 102.4 against Hendra/Nipah G protein and 14F3 against Cedar virus) were tested against the same panel of antigens alongside bat serum samples (supplementary material, figure S1). As negative controls, two wells per plate were filled with the same reagents but no serum (supplementary material, figure S19). MFI values from Ei. helvum serum samples against the Nipah virus G protein were previously shown to correlate with neutralization assay titration against Hendra virus and Nipah virus [53] and have been used in several studies to monitor seroprevalence and infer virus circulation in Ei. helvum bat populations (e.g. [70,92]). Peel et al. [53] suggested 500 MFI as a cut-off point for Nipah virus G protein assay to maximize sensitivity based on receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve analysis against neutralization data using serum from wild Ei. helvum. To date, we are not aware of similar validation data for other antigens or other bat species.A total of 413 serum samples were tested by MIA in duplicate against the panel of eight antigens alongside negative controls. Of these, 13 readings failed and 12 samples had to be discarded after quality control as they yielded fewer than 100 microspheres. After log10 transformation of the MFI values, we flagged a small number of samples with duplicate variation above 0.5 units but did not exclude them. Here we focus on the MIA data for the Nipah G and Ebola G antigens as these matched the vaccine antigens; other antibodies showed very little temporal variations (figure 3B and supplementary material, figure S2). full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Antibody response3.1.1.Nipah vaccineUsing a Luminex MIA, we observed increases in anti-Nipah-G antibody binding in all but one Ei. helvum bat from the Nipah vaccine group (figure 2A). When pooling the Ebola vaccine group and the PBS group to act as a control against the Nipah vaccine group, the net change in anti-Nipah-G binding from first to last sample was significantly greater in the Nipah vaccine group (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: W = 76, p = 0.0026, figure 2C). The range of MFI values in the Nipah vaccine group at the final time point was similar to those obtained with medium-to-high concentrations of the anti-Nipah-G monoclonal antibody 102.4 (supplementary material, figure S1). The MFI increase was already significant before the second injection (median increase of 1.0 log10 unit between the first sample and the last sample before the second injection in the Nipah group, −0.5 in the Ebola group and 0.0 in the PBS group), again confirmed statistically with a Wilcoxon test by pooling the Ebola and PBS groups as a control (W = 77, p = 0.0018, figure 2B). A linear mixed-effects model applied to the whole time series of log-transformed MFI against Nipah G (with vaccine group and time as fixed variables and bat identifier as a random variable) confirmed the significant effect of the Nipah vaccine (interaction between group and time: p < 10−4, see supplementary material, text S1). We also noted a negative correlation between the net change in anti-Nipah-G antibodies and their levels on the first day (figure 3A), whether across all bats (Pearson's r = −0.65, 95% CI [−0.85, −0.28]) or within the Nipah vaccine group (r = −0.90, 95% CI [−0.98, −0.44]). One bat in the PBS group showed a large increase in anti-Nipah-G binding at the last time point, possibly following exposure to a naturally occurring paramyxovirus shed by another bat in the same cage (figure 2A). Figure 2.Anti-Nipah-G antibody response in all treatment groups. (A) Time series of mean log10 (MFI) values against Nipah G, by species and experimental group. As no change in anti-Nipah-G antibodies was expected in the Ebola vaccine group, this group is considered a control in this figure. Each line represents one individual bat. Vertical dotted lines show the time of injections in each group. Samples and time points for which transcriptomic data were included in the differential gene expression analysis are shown in dark orange. (B) Box plot showing the log change in Nipah-G MFI values between the initial and third week (pre-booster) for each Eidolon helvum treatment group. Points represent the net change across that period for each Ei. helvum bat. (C) Box plot showing the log change in Nipah-G MFI values between the initial and eighth (final) week for each Ei. helvum treatment group. Points represent the net change across that period for each Ei. helvum bat.Figure 3.Serological response dynamics and correlations in Ei. helvum bats following Nipah-G vaccine delivery. (A) Association between the initial Nipah-G log-MFI value and the change in log-MFI values across the entire study period. Each dot represents a single Ei. helvum bat. (B) Box plot showing the changes in log-MFI values for all tested antigens across the entire study period for Ei. helvum. (C) Correlation between the MFI values from the Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay (MFI values against the Nipah-G antigen) and half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values from the lentivirus pseudotyped virus neutralization assay (serum dilution required to achieve 50% neutralization). The starting dilution was 50-fold; four sera with an IC50 below 50-fold are shown as points with a value of 50 (approx. 1.7 on the log scale).In our MIA panel of eight viral antigens from three henipaviruses and two filoviruses, the only other one to show a significant MFI increase in the Nipah vaccine group was the Hendra virus G protein, albeit to a lower extent than the Nipah virus G protein (figure 3B and supplementary material, figure S2).To test whether the bats produced neutralizing antibodies after vaccine exposure, a subset of 14 serum samples, collected at the end of the experiment and selected to cover the whole range of MFI values against the Nipah G antigen, were further tested by lentivirus pseudotyped virus neutralization assay [52] (supplementary material, text S2). There was a strong positive correlation between the measurements from the two assays (Spearman's ρ = 0.82, p = 0.0003, n = 14), indicating the presence of neutralizing antibodies in serum samples with MFI values above 200 units (figure 3C). Although we did not analyse changes in neutralizing antibodies across the experiment, we note that all eight bats in the Nipah vaccine group had detectable neutralizing antibodies by the end of the study (figure 3C).This pseudotype neutralizing threshold around 200 MFI units (2.3 log10 units) is slightly lower than the Nipah virus neutralization cut-off value of 500 MFI units (2.70 log10 units) previously established for Nipah G MIA in Ei. helvum [53]. The fact that several Ei. helvum bats in our study had initial MFI values above these thresholds (four above 500 MFI units and eight above 200; supplementary material, figure S3) is consistent with previous reports, for example 46% of wild-caught adult Ei. helvum from Ghana with values above 500 [36]. In the Nipah vaccine group, six out of seven Eidolon bats were initially below 500, and only two were still below this at the end of the experiment (figure 2).In contrast, none of the Epomophorus bats in the study had initial anti-Nipah-G binding levels above 500 MFI units. The two Epomophorus bats that survived for more than a week post prime injection showed a more pronounced pattern of seroconversion within days (figure 2A).3.1.2.Ebola vaccineIn sharp contrast to the response to the Nipah vaccine, there was no consistent increase in anti-Ebola antibodies in the Eidolon bats that received the Ebola vaccines (figure 4). The four Epomophorus bats that survived for at least a week post prime Ebola vaccine injection did, however, show large increases in anti-Ebola glycoprotein MFI values. The response to the Ebola vaccine in this species was similar in magnitude to the range of MFI values against serial dilutions of the anti-Ebola glycoprotein monoclonal antibody 5D2 (supplementary material, figure S1). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.Discussion4.1.Serological response to Nipah vaccineSerum antibody binding to bat henipavirus antigens using the Luminex MIA platform was previously validated in vitro against neutralization assays using Hendra and Nipah viruses [53]. While indicative of the protective function of antibodies in bats, it does not allow inference on the history of viral exposure or the kinetics of antibody production. Studying antibody kinetics in controlled experiments is key for interpreting wildlife serological data [68] but is challenging owing to the need of containment level 4 facilities. In this study, we measured antibody responses to Nipah and Ebola antigens in Ei. helvum and Ep. gambianus in an experimental setting to obtain positive controls for antibody levels in bats.MFI values observed in Ei. helvum after Nipah vaccine injection are comparable to those found in wild Ei. helvum populations [5,43,69] and to values obtained against monoclonal antibodies (supplementary material, figure S1). Furthermore, the steep increase in anti-Nipah-G antibody levels mirrors patterns observed in a captive colony of Ei. helvum bats in Ghana [70] with ongoing henipavirus circulation [71,72], where MFI increased by several thousand units within a three-month period [70]. Similar seroconversion was previously reported in Pteropus bats within two to four weeks after henipavirus infection [14,32]. While few studies have successfully detected paramyxovirus RNA or antibodies in Ep. gambianus (generally reporting lower prevalence than in Ei. helvum [38,43,44]), we observed a very strong antibody response in the few bats of this species that we were able to monitor.An important caveat is that, in the absence of a reliable antigen measurement assay for individual bats (owing to the low sensitivity of PCR on non-lethal bat samples [73]), we could not test bats for active henipavirus infection. The bats had unknown, probably diverse infection histories, as illustrated by their diverse pre-vaccine antibody levels. Thus, some of the observed seroconversions may have resulted from close-contact transmission of pre-existing viruses within the cages, such as the seroconversion recorded on the last time point in one individual from the PBS group. However, we previously found that such natural seroconversion events were rare in captive Ei. helvum, with a mean waiting time to seroconversion of 2.5 years for immunologically naive bats in a 100-strong captive colony [70].This study was not designed to measure antibody waning, but one Ei. helvum individual in the PBS group showed a steady decline in antibody levels over the eight weeks of sampling. Whereas previous studies inferred antibody decay in Ei. helvum over months or years, either indirectly from wild-caught bats of known age [69] or directly from longitudinal captive studies [70], this is the first study to document rapid decay on a weekly basis.4.2.Species-specific differences in the antibody response against the Ebola vaccineThe absence of detectable antibody response to the Ebola vaccine in Ei. helvum was unexpected and contrasts with the strong response to the same vaccine in Ep. gambianus. This discrepancy is notable because both species mounted a clear antibody response to a Nipah virus vaccine that used the same adenovirus vector. This vector does not display viral antigens directly but encodes the glycoprotein gene from the Ebola or Nipah virus, respectively, requiring host cell expression to induce an immune response.Although some studies have detected antibodies against Ebola viruses in a small number of wild-caught Ei. helvum [17,40], there is compelling experimental evidence that a mutation in the filovirus receptor NPC1 unique to this species of bats inhibits cell entry by Ebola virus in vitro [29]. However, we used an adenovirus vector which targets the coxsackie and adenovirus receptor (CAR), and we confirmed that the Ebola virus (EBOV) vaccine is able to enter Ei. helvum cells in vitro (supplementary material, figure S4). Another possible mechanism for the observed differences in antibody response to the Nipah and Ebola vaccines in Ei. helvum is the varying ability of tetherin (Bst2) to inhibit different viruses. Tetherin blocks viral particle release by linking them to the host cell membrane [74] and plays a key role in bat antiviral responses [75]. Interestingly, one study showed that tetherin inhibits Ebola virus replication [76], while another found that it inhibits Nipah but not Ebola virus replication [77] in Buettikofer's epauletted fruit bat (Epomops buettikoferi) cells. In our analysis, however, there was no evidence of differential expression of the tetherin gene Bst2.For the Nipah vaccine, MIA and a pseudotyped virus neutralization assay showed concordant results. A similar agreement (albeit with negative results only) was observed for the Ebola vaccine in Ei. helvum. In contrast, we noted a discordant antibody result for Ep. gambianus vaccinated against Ebola: the MIA detected high MFI signal for antibody binding to the Ebola GP, yet these antibodies failed to neutralize a corresponding pseudotyped virus. Similar discordances between Ebola virus GP binding antibodies and virus neutralization titres have been made in experimental vaccination studies in animals and people as well as studies from naturally infected human survivors [78,79]. Our own results suggest that Ep. gambianus may produce GP-specific antibodies that are reactive to non-neutralizing epitopes on the protein. While non-neutralizing antibodies may not directly block viral entry, they can still play a role in immune response through Fc-mediated effector functions, such as phagocytosis or natural killer (NK) cell activation [80]. In the context of Ebola virus, both neutralizing and non-neutralizing antibodies have been associated with protection from infection [81]. However, it is important to note that our understanding of the kinetics and function of antibodies during and after viral infection in bats is limited. Further studies are needed to assess whether the antibodies detected in Ep. gambianus provide protection against Ebola virus.We acknowledge that the statistical power of this study was limited by the small number of animals, especially Ep. gambianus, where the few surviving individuals may not be representative of the species as a whole. Additionally, the unavailability of positive control serum from bats with known Ebola virus infection remains a significant challenge for assay validation. Future technical work should focus on optimizing serological assays, for instance by investigating the impact of the Ebola GP mucin-like domain on antigen presentation, to better estimate the sensitivity and specificity of these tools in bats.4.3.Differential gene expression4.3.1.Gene expression response in the Ebola vaccine groupBy comparing the gene expression profiles between the Ei. helvum Ebola and Nipah vaccine groups, we aimed to identify potential differences that could explain the observed variation in antibody production. One key finding when comparing each vaccine group to the control individual was that several GO terms related to Th cell differentiation were over-represented in the Ebola vaccine group, while this was not observed in the Nipah vaccine group. Th cells play a crucial role in immune function, differentiating into Th1 or Th2 subtypes, each promoting different immune responses. Th1 differentiation, typically driven by intracellular pathogens, is associated with IFN-γ and IL-12 secretion [82]. In contrast, Th2 cells, typically stimulated by extracellular antigens, help initiate the humoral immune response by activating naive B cells to secrete IgM and other antibodies such as IgA, IgE and IgG [82]. Owing to limited detection of cytokine transcripts, we were unable to determine which Th cell subtypes predominated in the Ebola vaccine group. As a result, we cannot conclude whether a potential shift towards cellular immunity,…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 4.4.ConclusionThis study provides rare insight into the in vivo immune responses in two species of African fruit bat following exposure to Ebola or Nipah virus antigens. Remarkably, one bat species (Ep. gambianus) developed detectable antibodies against both virus antigens, while the other bat species (Ei. helvum) only developed antibodies against Nipah virus antigens. A simultaneous transcriptome analysis in Ei. helvum revealed that few antiviral genes and pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Nipah vaccine, while genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Ebola vaccine. We acknowledge important limitations in our study design, notably the absence of female bats (to minimize complications caused by pregnancy) and the rapid depletion of Epomophorus bats (potentially introducing a survivorship bias), which will have to be addressed in future studies. Our findings, while preliminary, highlight immune mechanisms that might explain the specificity of host–virus associations in bats.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionThe role of bats as natural reservoirs for emerging zoonotic viruses has become a major concern in the last 20 years [1,2]. This has motivated unprecedented research effort into bat immunology, with approaches including experimental infections in high-containment facilities, the development of bat cell lines for in vitro immunoassays and bioinformatic analysis of bat genome and transcriptome sequences [3]. Recent investigations have identified unique adaptations of the innate immune system in bats which may explain how they can host viruses with high mortality in other species without presenting clinical disease [4]. In contrast, the adaptive immune system of bats remains poorly understood [3].Virus-specific antibody measurement is routinely used as a marker of viral exposure in wild-caught bats and plays a crucial role in the surveillance of wildlife pathogens of zoonotic risk [5]. However, interpreting these assays and inferring seroprevalence in bat populations is hindered by a lack of understanding of the kinetics and function of antibodies during or after viral infection in bats [3,6]. A review of experimental infection and vaccination in bats noted that antibody responses were variable, with some animals remaining immune to viral challenge even in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibodies [7]. In addition, results from experimental infections appear to vary between bat species and viral infections [8]. More detailed information on kinetics, magnitude and functionality of the humoral immune response in different bat species would facilitate the interpretation of serological data from the wild [9].Henipaviruses (family Paramyxoviridae) [10–14] and Ebola viruses (family Filoviridae) [15–21] have caused repeated deadly outbreaks in people and domestic animals on three continents [22–25], and both groups have been linked to fruit bat hosts from the Pteropodidae family. This family consists of nearly 200 species that are widely distributed in tropical regions in Africa, Asia, Australia and many Pacific and Indian Ocean islands [26]. Serological data from wild bats have revealed differences in antibody levels against henipaviruses and filoviruses in fruit bat species with overlapping distributions [19,27,28], yet little is known about the mechanisms behind host-specificity (but see [29]).Experimental infections with henipaviruses in a few bat species have confirmed the production of serum antibodies and the excretion of virus in urine without developing apparent clinical disease [14,30–32]. Experimental infections with Ebola viruses in the Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) likewise yielded antibodies without apparent clinical disease, but no viraemia was recorded aside from low levels of viral RNA detection [33,34]. The authors concluded that this bat species is an unlikely source of Ebola virus spillover in nature. While focusing on virus and antibody detection, none of these studies provided further characterization of the immune response of live bats following viral exposure. Extending these experimental studies to other pairs of bat and virus species is made extremely difficult and costly by biocontainment imperatives, creating a need for alternative approaches.As a new step towards unravelling the kinetics of the adaptive antiviral immune response of bats in vivo, we designed an experiment with two African fruit bat species, using recombinant vaccines against Ebola and Nipah viruses as a tool to alleviate the biosafety constraints inherent to the study of filoviruses and henipaviruses. The two bat species, Eidolon helvum and Epomophorus gambianus, were chosen for their documented association with henipaviruses and filoviruses, respectively. The straw-coloured fruit bat, Ei. helvum, spans most of subtropical Africa, forming large, migratory and panmictic colonies [35–37], with estimates of seroprevalence against henipaviruses around 40% across its range [36] and repeated detection of viral RNA from multiple paramyxoviruses [36,38]. Antibodies against Ebola virus have also been detected in Ei. helvum [17,20,21,39–41], but the interpretation remains speculative in the absence of further validation. The Gambian epauletted fruit bat, Ep. gambianus, while less gregarious, is often sympatric with Ei. helvum [42]. Detection of paramyxovirus RNA or antibodies is rare in this species [38,43,44]. Antibodies against filoviruses have been detected in wild Ep. gambianus on several occasions [18,21,39,41], but active infection has never been confirmed. To date, no filovirus RNA has been found in either bat species, and the sensitivity and specificity of serological assays for antibodies against Ebola virus in bats remain to be assessed. These two species of fruit bat thus provide a unique system to study host–virus specificity: despite overlapping geographic distributions, serological surveys suggest they may be hosts to different subsets of zoonotic viruses and might, therefore, respond differently to virus inoculation.The objectives of this study were twofold. First, we wanted to compare the dynamics of antibody production in the two bat species in response to vaccine exposure, as a way to improve the interpretation of bat virus serological data from field studies. We hypothesized that recombinant vaccines expressing Nipah or Ebola virus antigens (which had only just become available for research purposes at the time of planning this study [45,46]) would mimic virus inoculation without the need to use live virus, eliciting antibody production comparable to levels observed in the field and revealing differences in virus-specific response between bat species. Our second objective was to identify adaptive immune pathways involved in antiviral response and antibody production in bats, by measuring changes in gene expression for four weeks in a subset of Ei. helvum bats from each vaccine group. 2.Experimental set-upHere, we outline the experimental set-up, focusing on the animal work; the full ‘Material and methods’ are presented in §5. After capture and selection of healthy adult males, 19 Ei. helvum and 14 Ep. gambianus bats were individually tagged with intradermal microchips and were placed in cages (80 × 80 × 80 cm) in single-species groups of up to five bats for the rest of the study (two months). Bats from each species were split into three groups to receive one of three treatments: Ebola vaccine, Nipah vaccine or saline injections. The first group (nEidolon = 8, nEpomophorus = 6) received an intramuscular dose of recombinant chimpanzee adenovirus vaccine (ChAdOx1) encoding the Orthoebolavirus zairense glycoprotein (hereafter Ebola virus GP protein), followed four weeks later by an intramuscular dose of modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) vaccine encoding the same Ebola virus GP protein, following a previously published protocol [47]. title_original: Serological and transcriptomic response of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the serological and transcriptomic immune responses of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens, addressing the lack of in vivo immunological studies on bat antibodies against zoonotic viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in experimental facilities in Ghana with 19 African straw-coloured fruit bats (Ei. gambianus) captured from their roosts in Accra, and samples were collected over two months with individuals placed in single-species groups of up to five bats.
analysis.methods: Antibody responses to Nipah and Ebola antigens were measured using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay, and transcriptomic data were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and pathways in response to the vaccines.
analysis.main_results: The Nipah vaccine group showed a significant increase in anti-Nipah-G antibody binding compared to the PBS group (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: W = 76, p = 0.0026), with MFI values comparable to those of a monoclonal antibody. A linear mixed-effects model confirmed the significant effect of the Nipah vaccine on antibody levels (p < 10−4).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed antibody kinetics provide insights into the in vivo immune response to Nipah virus antigens in bats, highlighting the potential of serological markers for surveillance of zoonotic pathogens, though they do not confirm viral exposure or production kinetics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings contribute to understanding the immune responses of bats to Nipah virus antigens, which is critical for improving surveillance strategies and developing vaccines against zoonotic pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by the use of a small sample size and the challenges of maintaining containment level 4 facilities, but the evidence is moderate due to the controlled experimental setting and statistical validation of results.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the serological and transcriptomic immune responses of African fruit bats to recombinant vaccines expressing Nipah or Ebola virus antigens. Bats were captured in Ghana and housed in controlled environments for two months. Antibody responses were measured using a Luminex-based assay, and transcriptomic data were analyzed to identify gene expression changes. The Nipah vaccine group showed a significant increase in anti-Nipah-G antibody binding compared to the PBS control group, with MFI values comparable to monoclonal antibody levels. A linear mixed-effects model confirmed the vaccine's effect on antibody levels. The results suggest that serological markers can inform surveillance of zoonotic pathogens, though they do not confirm viral exposure. The study's evidence is moderate due to its controlled experimental design and statistical validation, despite limitations in sample size and the need for containment level 4 facilities.
