full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. TBEV, tick-borne encephalitis virus. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article typically invade the central nerve system, whereas yellow fever virus and DENV do not17. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. The use of fixed-dose combinations (such as those used in the treatment of HIV infections) would be ideal. Yet, in outbreak situation with new pathogens, there will be insufficient time to develop such fixed-dose combinations; co-administration of individual drugs would therefore represent a more practical approach. full_text_sections.full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Nipah virus (Henipavirus nipahense), Nipah virus infection and disease. The central question is the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus, with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families, or even crossing viral families.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses, including Nipah virus. It discusses the rationale for developing BSAs and outlines the biological determinants underlying their antiviral spectrum. The review does not explicitly report on meta-analysis or pooled estimates but provides a non-exhaustive overview of existing and experimental drugs.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the development of broader-acting small molecule antivirals is essential to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. It highlights that newly emerging viruses are likely to belong to known viral families, supporting the strategy of developing BSAs. The review also outlines the clinical development frameworks required to evaluate such drugs, particularly in outbreaks.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of effective antiviral therapeutics for many RNA viruses, including Nipah virus, as a major evidence gap. It notes that while advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing have expanded our understanding of viral diversity, the development of BSAs remains limited. The review also highlights the need for more research on the biological determinants that underlie the antiviral spectrum of these drugs.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the need for sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery, particularly for RNA viruses like Nipah virus. It suggests that developing potent, safe, and orally available antivirals is crucial for both treating known viral infections and responding rapidly to outbreaks. The review also outlines the importance of clinical development frameworks tailored for BSAs.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a focus on Nipah virus. It highlights the lack of effective antiviral treatments for many RNA viruses, including Nipah, and underscores the importance of creating drugs with activity spanning multiple genera or families. The review discusses the rationale for BSAs, the biological factors influencing their antiviral spectrum, and the clinical frameworks needed to evaluate them. It also stresses the need for investment in antiviral research to address current medical needs and improve pandemic preparedness. The review identifies gaps in understanding the mechanisms of antiviral action and the need for more targeted research on BSAs.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本评论聚焦于尼帕病毒(亨尼帕病毒 nipahense)病毒、尼帕病毒病毒感染及其疾病。核心问题是开发针对RNA病毒的广谱直接作用抗病毒药物药物(BSAs),包括尼帕病毒病毒,其活性可覆盖多个属、整个科甚至跨越病毒科。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本评论是对针对RNA病毒(包括尼帕病毒病毒)的已批准和正在研究的抗病毒药物药物的系统性概述。它讨论了开发BSAs的合理性,并概述了这些药物广谱活性背后的生物学决定因素。本评论并未明确报告元分析或汇总估计,而是提供了现有和实验性药物的非详尽概述。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论得出结论,开发具有广谱作用的小分子抗病毒药物药物对于应对当前未满足的医疗需求以及加强流行病和大流行病的应对能力至关重要。它指出,新出现的病毒很可能属于已知的病毒科,这支持了开发BSAs的策略。本评论还概述了评估此类药物所需的临床开发框架,特别是在暴发方面。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本评论指出了许多RNA病毒(包括尼帕病毒病毒)缺乏有效抗病毒药物治疗药物,这是一个主要的证据缺口。它指出,尽管在宏基因组学和高通量测序方面的进展扩展了我们对病毒多样性的理解,但BSAs的开发仍受到限制。本评论还强调了需要更多研究来探讨这些药物广谱活性背后的生物学决定因素。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本评论强调了持续投资抗病毒药物药物发现的必要性,特别是针对如尼帕病毒病毒等RNA病毒。它建议开发强效、安全且口服可用的抗病毒药物药物对于治疗已知病毒感染和快速应对暴发至关重要。本评论还概述了为BSAs量身定制的临床开发框架的重要性。

title: Iterative Co‐Development of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment Operational Process and Tool Through Incorporating Information From Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia

source_records.title: Iterative Co‐Development of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment Operational Process and Tool Through Incorporating Information From Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia
Iterative Co‐Development of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment Operational Process and Tool Through Incorporating Information From Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia

full_text: ABSTRACTIntroductionZoonotic diseases pose risks to human, animal, and ecosystem health; effective management relies on coordinated actions across sectors. Although One Health principles promote collaboration across sectors, operational tools for multisectoral risk assessment (RA) are lacking. Therefore, the Tripartite (FAO, WHO, and WOAH) developed the first‐ever One Health operational tool for Joint Risk Assessment (JRA‐OT), with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. This article describes how information from pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia contributed to informing co‐development of the final JRA process and tool.MethodsThree in‐person meetings with international RA and zoonotic disease experts with a One Health background were convened in Rome, Italy, to co‐develop the methodology (November 2017, September 2018) and incorporate pilot feedback (February 2020). Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. The pilot workshops described here were conducted in Indonesia (March 2018), the United Republic of Tanzania (March 2019), and Georgia (July 2019), and feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat.ResultsThese pilot workshops demonstrated JRA's utility and provided critical information for improvements. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. The process serves as a model for co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools.Keywords: Joint Operational Tools, One Health, risk assessment, zoonoses Piloting of the Tripartite Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) process and tool in countries provided feedback for improvement, evidence‐based estimates of national risks from priority zoonotic diseases, and practical training of national facilitators. The JRA offers simple step‐by‐step guidance to countries wishing to undertake joint qualitative risk assessments. 2.Methods2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security and disaster services.Function within existing zoonotic disease management and One Health governance infrastructures.Be adaptable to the relevant contextBe usable by governments, academia, or anyone wishing to conduct RA jointly across sectors.Support international sector‐specific RA and health security frameworks (e.g., International Health Regulations [9], WHO Rapid RA [4], WOAH Import Risk Analysis [5], FAO draft Guidelines on Rapid RA [now published [6]]).Once the new basic JRA process and tool were agreed, they were tested during (1) two international in‐person workshops in Rome, Italy (November 2017, September 2018), bringing together international multisectoral RA experts from different geographical regions selected by the three organizations to review and fine‐tune the methodology, and (2) 15 country pilots conducted between March 2018 and December 2019 (Figure 1), which guided iterative updates. All pilots were in‐person and had the same direct and indirect objectives (Table 1). A final in‐person expert consultation was held in Rome, Italy (February 2020), and the JRA‐OT was published in December 2020 [8]. The development timeline is depicted in Figure 2.FIGURE 1Joint Risk Assessment pilot countries.TABLE 1Objectives of the Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) pilot workshops.Direct objectivesIndirect objectives Build capacity through training a pool of national facilitators to operationalize the JRA tool at national and subnational levelsProvide likelihood and impact estimates for risk assessment questions on priority hazardsAssess the usefulness of the JRA and consider its sustained useCollect feedback to improve interim versions of the JRA Enhance coordination and trust among relevant stakeholdersFacilitate official and unofficial communication and information sharing among stakeholdersAdvocate for allocation of resources FIGURE 2Development timeline of the Joint Risk Assessment operational tool.2.2.Pilot WorkshopsFor each of the 15 pilot workshops, all relevant ministries, particularly those responsible for animal health and public health, were encouraged to engage through outreach by FAO and WHO country offices. Tripartite central, regional, and country office staff supported the workshops as external facilitators. All pilots, aside from the Indonesian pilot where the risk framing was conducted during the workshop, followed the six steps, below and in Figure 3, adapted from common RA processes used in public health, animal health, and/or environmental RA: Hazard identification: Technical staff and decision‐makers in engaged ministries (hereafter, “ministries”) agreed on national priority endemic, epidemic, or emerging zoonotic hazards, up to 6 months prior to the workshop. Risk framing: Once the hazards were agreed, ministerial decision‐makers characterized the scope, purpose, and objectives of the assessment on the basis of government strategy and policy to ensure the JRA process remained efficient and focused on critical government needs. Selection of participants and national staff: After Steps 1 and 2, ministries identified participants based on the identified hazards and risk framing and selected staff to facilitate the planning and implementation of the pilot and future JRAs (hereafter, “national facilitators”). A JRA lead was agreed among ministries. High‐level ministerial participation was encouraged for workshop Days 0 and 3. Day 0: National facilitators finalized the risk framing and were trained on the JRA process and tool by the external facilitators. Days 1–2: The JRA was introduced and undertaken by participants, led by the national facilitators and supported by external facilitators. Small groups each focused on one identified hazard using information brought to the workshop and presented the outcome of each step in plenary. Substantial time was dedicated to plenary discussion and questions, covering both the technical assessments and the JRA process itself. Day 3: Each group presented final results in plenary. Participants, including decision‐makers, considered existing national zoonotic disease and One Health infrastructure and options for governance of routine JRA leadership and implementation, and identified what criteria would trigger conducting or updating a JRA.FIGURE 3Schematic of the final Joint Risk Assessment process applied during national JRA pilots. Steps are fully described in WHO et al. [8].2.3.Data Capture, Analysis, and IntegrationFrom each pilot's planning period through to the end of each workshop, constraints, challenges, and proposed solutions gleaned from plenary and group workshop discussions, and verbal feedback from participants and national facilitators were captured in written notes taken by the external facilitators. Standardized written feedback on the process, tool, and workshop was requested anonymously from attendees using a questionnaire (Pilot Feedback Form; see Supporting Information). Completion of questionnaires was optional.At the end of each workshop day, the external and national facilitators gathered to discuss how the day went and share the feedback received so far. Potential modifications to the JRA based on captured information and challenges were continually discussed among the pilot facilitators and the Tripartite focal points leading the development of the JRA (hereafter, JRA Secretariat). After each pilot workshop, the JRA Secretariat met virtually to revisit the feedback received and suggest corrective actions to the tool and process accordingly. On the basis of importance, urgency, and complexity, straightforward and uncontroversial corrections were made by the JRA Secretariat immediately and prior to the next workshop, whereas more complex issues were collected in a list of discussion points and brought forward to expert review and decision during the final expert workshop held in Rome (September 2018). As pilots were conducted, the JRA Secretariat noted that challenges fell into three categories: Challenges that were consistent across countries, such as misleading or unclear text, and definitely required changing to ensure comprehension.Challenges that varied across countries and could not be improved in a generic way and were best managed by stating in JRA materials that these aspects are country‐specific and would be managed during national JRAs.Challenges that fell outside the scope of the JRA process and would not be useful to address in the tool.2.4.Country Pilot Selection for This ManuscriptThe pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia (Table 2 and further described chronologically below) were purposively selected by the JRA Secretariat for further description in this manuscript, based on (1) each being the first country in its geographical region to conduct a JRA pilot and (2) the level of contribution the country's findings had in informing the final JRA content and processes.TABLE 2Summary of Joint Risk Assessment pilot workshops in Indonesia, Tanzania, and Georgia.IndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaDatesMarch 13–16, 2018March 25–28, 2019July 2–5, 2019LocationBogorDar es SalaamKakhetiNumber of participants642425Hazards assessedZoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Leptospira interrogans Zoonotic influenza viruses, rabies virus, Bacillus anthracis Rabies virus, Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus Supplementary Materials Supporting File: puh270398‐sup‐0001‐SuppMat.pdf. 3.Results3.1.IndonesiaThe Indonesian JRA pilot workshop was the first JRA pilot conducted and took place in Bogor on March 13–16, 2018. The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. Leveraging the strong multisectoral engagement and zoonotic disease experience of local partners facilitated the emergence of important lessons. Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indon…

After each pilot workshop, the JRA Secretariat met virtually to revisit the feedback received and suggest corrective actions to the tool and process accordingly. On the basis of importance, urgency, and complexity, straightforward and uncontroversial corrections were made by the JRA Secretariat immediately and prior to the next workshop, whereas more complex issues were collected in a list of discussion points and brought forward to expert review and decision during the final expert workshop held in Rome (September 2018). As pilots were conducted, the JRA Secretariat noted that challenges fell into three categories: Challenges that were consistent across countries, such as misleading or unclear text, and definitely required changing to ensure comprehension.Challenges that varied across countries and could not be improved in a generic way and were best managed by stating in JRA materials that these aspects are country‐specific and would be managed during national JRAs.Challenges that fell outside the scope of the JRA process and would not be useful to address in the tool.2.4.Country Pilot Selection for This ManuscriptThe pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia (Table 2 and further described chronologically below) were purposively selected by the JRA Secretariat for further description in this manuscript, based on…
full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.IndonesiaThe Indonesian JRA pilot workshop was the first JRA pilot conducted and took place in Bogor on March 13–16, 2018. The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces. Five hazards (zoonotic influenza viruses in three different contexts, rabies virus, and Leptospira interrogans) were assessed. Leveraging the strong multisectoral engagement and zoonotic disease experience of local partners facilitated the emergence of important lessons. Because Indonesia was the first pilot, these lessons greatly impacted the JRA process and tool and all subsequent pilots.The Indonesia pilot generated key findings related to risk framing, pre‐workshop training, political will, and subnational involvement.3.1.1.Introducing a Risk‐Framing StepInitially, the draft JRA process did not include a step where decision‐makers could provide strategic and policy‐related inputs to frame the assessment. As such, Indonesian participants and facilitators found they had to identify the assessment's scope and policy objectives as a first step of the group work. This was time‐consuming and only possible because ministerial decision‐makers were present and engaged to advise. The national facilitators suggested that ministerial decision‐makers could undertake this step prior to the workshop, inspiring the addition of the pre‐pilot risk‐framing step to the final JRA.3.1.2.Adding a 1‐Day Pre‐Workshop Training for National FacilitatorsInitially, the “Day 0 national facilitators” training was also not part of the JRA process. Proactively, the Indonesian organizers initiated a full‐day pre‐pilot meeting of the JRA Secretariat and national technical staff to familiarize national facilitators with the JRA steps and to review the workshop objectives. These included staff from the provinces, and hereafter, the term “national facilitators” is inclusive of subnational staff. The entire team agreed that this pre‐pilot meeting was critical to the success of the workshop as it ensured that national facilitators (1) understood the JRA principles, step‐wise process, and tool; (2) practiced facilitation skills with support from the external facilitators prior to the workshop; and (3) could take a leading role in facilitation the next day. Skilled national facilitators would not only bring local context and perspectives but also create JRA sustainability, as external facilitators would no longer be needed for subsequent national and subnational JRAs. Subsequently, “Day 0” was incorporated for all future pilots, with national facilitators and JRA Secretariat attending Days 0–3 and all other participants attending Days 1–3. “Day 0” is not included in the tool as the JRA is meant to be done autonomously by countries, that is, once facilitators are familiar with the JRA tool and process.3.1.3.Importance of Political Will for JRA SuccessThe Government of Indonesia (GOI) was the first government to request a JRA workshop in 2017. The Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Agriculture (MoA), and Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture (Kemenko PMK) were strongly involved in planning and implementation. Director‐level representatives from these agencies were present during the entire workshop, contributed operationally to discussions, and were available to support the unanticipated risk‐framing activity. Not only did the Director General of MoH Prevention and Disease Control open the JRA, but he also requested a side meeting with the JRA Secretariat to show his direct support and appreciation of the JRA initiative and One Health approaches in general. The team agreed that this high‐level political engagement, as well as leveraging the strong national One Health culture, facilitated the later implementation of JRAs at national and subnational levels [10, 11]. The MoH proposed translating and adapting the tool further for the Indonesian context and embedding JRA within the national and provincial frameworks for zoonoses and other emerging infectious diseases based on the existing infrastructure and legal framework. This would be coordinated centrally by Kemenko PMK in collaboration with MoH, MoA, and Ministry of Environment and Forestry. Political will is now highlighted in the final JRA tool as a key element for enhancing the JRA success.3.1.4.Subnational Involvement for Field‐Context and to Ensure Relevance of OutputsThe proactive inclusion of participants from three provinces in the workshop permitted separate assessments of influenza viruses in three different contexts by participants living in those contexts. This allowed nuanced RA and creation of risk management options specific to their epidemiological and cultural context. It emphasized both that not all risks are national, and that local knowledge is critical to assessment of context‐specific risks. Participants were able to then implement subsequent provincial assessments autonomously.3.1.5.Subsequent JRA Implementation in IndonesiaTo further support subnational JRAs, Indonesia initiated national JRA Training of Trainers (ToTs) activities in 2020 followed by ToTs in 10 provinces in 2021, which benefitted from the clear, stepwise guidance provided by the JRA‐OT. Subsequent JRAs applied the revised final tool and operational process and were conducted for SARS‐CoV‐2 virus (2021), Mycobacterium bovis (2022), avian influenza viruses (2022, 2023), rabies virus (2023), and Nipah virus (2026).3.2.United Republic of TanzaniaThe workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania, hereafter referred to as “Tanzania,” took place 1 year later, in Dar es Salaam on March 25–28, 2019. Tanzania was the first African country to conduct a JRA pilot workshop. Twenty‐four representatives of diverse government agencies, including disaster management, at central and subnational levels (e.g., Zanzibar), the One Health Coordination Desk (OHCD), and academic institutions participated during Days 1–3, whereas the JRA Secretariat, national facilitators, the One Health Coordinator, and the Minister of Health also attended Day 0 for the national facilitator training. Zoonotic influenza virus, Bacillus anthracis, and rabies virus were chosen as priority hazards. Both Tanzania's experience managing zoonotic diseases and the active OHCD for multisectoral coordination, which had experience organizing One Health trainings, facilitated success in pre‐pilot activities and workshop planning.The Tanzania pilot validated key findings from the Indonesia pilot. As with Indonesia, Tanzanian participants suggested organizing nationally led ToT at the central and subnational levels. The importance of political will and high‐level input was affirmed, with ministerial participation on all 4 days of the workshop. Zanzibar was highlighted as a priority setting for implementing subnational JRAs, confirming their importance and value. Further findings included the use of virtual risk framing and using existing structures to sustain JRA implementation.3.2.1.Risk Framing Through Virtual ConsultationTanzania was one of the first countries to conduct a risk framing and the first done virtually with support from the JRA Secretariat. Practical lessons were learned about risk‐framing implementation, for example, that each hazard should be framed separately, and that the risk‐framing template should contain only information strictly necessary to focus the RA. Importantly, Tanzania demonstrated that the risk framing was effectively done virtually, and benefits of the virtual risk‐framing meeting were noted by the JRA Secretariat.3.2.2.Utilizing the Existing Multisectoral Coordination Mechanism as JRA Steering CommitteeAlready in 2015, Tanzania had developed and implemented its Prime Ministerial level One Health Strategic Plan and had establ…
full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionTo address the lack of One Health operational tools to guide joint, multisectoral RA for zoonotic disease threats, the Tripartite co‐developed the JRA‐OT with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts. Between 2015 and 2020, feedback was incorporated iteratively into the JRA‐OT by a Tripartite Secretariat to generate the final version [8] published in 2020.Pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia were the first to be conducted in their respective geographical regions and generated key lessons that were particularly important for informing the final tool and, thus, were selected for detailed description in this manuscript. There was much overlap across the findings from these countries, suggesting that they also represented countries generally. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culture from the three countries, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) inclusion of all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and ToTs (Table 3).TABLE 3Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed across pilots and integrated into the final Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) tool and process.Summary of key lessons learned or confirmed through JRA pilotsLesson learned inIndonesiaTanzaniaGeorgiaValue of policy‐level risk framing (in person or online)xxxImportance of political will and leveraging existing One Health culturexxxNeed for subnational engagementxxxImportance of including all relevant sectorsxNecessity of providing clear, stepwise operational guidance and training of trainersxx4.1.Value of Policy‐Level Risk FramingOne of the most important findings across pilots was the need for a formal risk‐framing process led by decision‐makers ahead of the workshop. In Indonesia, participants realized that defining the scope, objectives, and policy priorities during the workshop itself was inefficient and only possible because senior officials were present. Tanzania further demonstrated that risk framing could be conducted effectively through virtual consultations and highlighted the importance of framing each hazard separately. In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al. [14]. Indonesia benefited from strong ministerial engagement and an established One Health governance structure, which later supported national and provincial JRA expansion. Tanzania's politically supported OHCD played a central role in organizing and sustaining JRA activities, whereas ministerial participation throughout the workshop reinforced national ownership. Similarly, Georgia's existing One Health Division within the NCDC facilitated planning, coordination, and policy relevance. Across pilots, political support increased participant engagement, improved alignment with national priorities, and facilitated translating JRA findings into action.4.3.Need for Subnational EngagementThe pilots consistently demonstrated that involving subnational participants improved the relevance and practicality of assessments. During pilots, subnational participants were noted to be especially engaged and motivated to act. In Indonesia, representatives from three provinces assessed influenza risks in their own local contexts, enabling development of tailored risk management strategies and demonstrating that zoonotic risks are often context‐specific rather than purely national. Tanzania identified Zanzibar as a priority setting for future subnational JRAs, highlighting the value of localized implementation. In Georgia, regional participants emphasized differences in rabies epidemiology across areas and proposed immediate use of JRA methods at the subnational level. Overall, the pilots showed that subnational participation strengthens contextual understanding, improves local ownership, and supports implementation of locally relevant mitigation measures.4.4.Inclusion of all Relevant SectorsAnother key lesson was the importance of ensuring representation from all relevant sectors in JRA workshops. Georgia particularly illustrated this challenge when the absence of the wildlife sector limited discussions on rabies risks involving wildlife transmission. This experience demonstrated that gaps in sectoral participation can reduce the completeness and quality of assessments. However, it also showed that the JRA process itself can help identify missing stakeholders and strengthen multisectoral collaboration over time. Across pilots, broad participation from human health, animal health, environment, disaster management, and other sectors was recognized as essential for comprehensive RA and effective One Health coordination for zoonotic diseases.4.5.Necessity of Clear, Stepwise Operational Guidance, and ToTsThe pilots highlighted the need for practical, stepwise operational guidance and strong national facilitation capacity. Indonesia pioneered the Day 0 national facilitator training, which became a standard feature of subsequent JRAs. This training helped facilitators understand the methodology, practice facilitation skills, and eventually lead workshops independently, reducing reliance on external experts. Pilots in Tanzania and Georgia validated the value of this approach, with national facilitators increasingly taking ownership of workshop implementation. The Georgia pilot highlighted the need for clearer guidance on hazard selection and joint risk‐framing procedures that were then added into the tool. In both Indonesia and Tanzania, participants recommended national and subnational ToT programs to build sustainable in‐country expertise. Together, these experiences emphasized that successful JRA implementation depends not only on the tool itself, but also on clear, stepwise operational guidance, standardized processes, and national capacity building.After review and discussion of these key lessons learned, the JRA Secretariat made the following revisions to the JRA tool and process: (1) introduction of a dedicated pre‐workshop risk‐framing Step 2 in the JRA process, led by decision‐makers, including a template for framing risks related to each hazard identified in Step 1; (2) highlighting the importance of political will and the opportunity to leverage existing national One Health structures to sustainably implement JRA; and (3) highlighting the importance of prospective inclusion of all relevant sectors, with participation of national and subnational levels, especially relevant in Step 3 where participants are being identified. The full‐day training for national facilitators on Day 0 was added to planning for all future workshops to foster ownership in country pilots, familiarize national facilitators, including subnational staff, with the JRA steps and some basic facilitation principles and review the workshop objectives.All three countries saw the JRA as an opportunity to operationalize One Health strategies while producing practical, tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication.The evidence‐based JRA output served as advocacy to secure high‐level commitment and resources for risk mitigation. Participants from different sectors often still did not know each other, despite ongoing multisectoral activities and high levels of One Health awareness further emphasized the need to strengthen routine collaborative activities, such as JRA.The JRA process can present challenges. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionKnowledge iteratively gained during pilots was critical to enhance the usefulness and effectiveness of the JRA process and tool, and ownership by different sectors. Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing. Sustained political commitment and established One Health coordination mechanisms were critical enablers of successful JRA implementation and long‐term national ownership. Inclusion of subnational actors and all relevant sectors significantly improved the contextual relevance, completeness, and operational value of RAs.The pilots showed that JRAs can serve not only as technical tools for RA, but also as mechanisms for strengthening multisectoral collaboration, information sharing, and One Health governance. Standardized operational guidance, facilitator training, and nationally led ToTs were essential for building sustainable country capacity and reducing reliance on external support.The JRA was co‐developed iteratively and inclusively across countries, sectors, and scales to meet objectives laid down by national governments and experts in RA and zoonotic diseases to assess risks, and thus models One Health best practice in both content and process and ensures ownership by the different sectors. The methodology can be used as a model for development of other multisectoral operational processes and tools. The JRA's inclusive, systematic, and evidence‐based RA process is now available to all countries, improving management of critical national zoonotic disease risks.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionActions and policies to identify, assess, manage, and reduce risks from zoonotic diseases benefit from functional collaboration and engagement across stakeholders and sectors, including academia, the private sector, local communities, and government ministries responsible for human health, animal health, food safety, wildlife, environment, trade, education, security and disasters, and the economy [1]. Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors. Due to its sensitive nature, information related to zoonotic diseases can potentially influence consumer behavior and/or compromise a country's economy or tourism if made public. Sharing such information between sectors often must be authorized and may be restricted or delayed, especially in the absence of clear sharing mechanisms or policies. Further, although countries could access sector‐specific RA methodologies and processes, they encountered challenges in assessing risks jointly when encountering differing steps and terminology across RA methods and the reluctance of sectors to agree on an approach unfamiliar to them in the absence of expert guidance. These countries requested assistance from the Tripartite [3] to identify and propose a technically sound approach to conducting joint, multisectoral zoonotic disease RA.Technical aspects of estimating risks are, in principle, similar across RA methods, and it is normally possible to incorporate information from other sectors during sector‐specific zoonotic disease RAs. However, each sector‐specific method evolved to achieve different objectives. Consequently, RA methods are operationally different, do not easily align, and do not lend themselves to joint use. Although many institutions and agencies publish RA reports for zoonotic diseases, an extensive search of published guidance for conducting zoonotic disease RA across health‐related disciplines identified only sector‐specific tools available at that time. Further, the guidance from WHO [4], WOAH [5](updated in 2024) and FAO [6](available internally but unpublished at the time) referred to assessment for zoonotic diseases but had been developed exclusively by and for the human health and animal health sectors, respectively. The RA procedures of the Codex Alimentarius Commission [7] were also available but primarily focused on quantitative assessment of contaminants in food and were not practical for use by countries. To fill this gap, the Tripartite convened international RA experts and pilot countries to iteratively co‐develop the first‐ever One Health operational tool for conducting zoonotic disease RA jointly across sectors.The Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) was published as the Joint Risk Assessment Operational Tool (JRA‐OT) in 2020 [8], as one of the operational tools supporting the Tripartite Zoonoses Guide [1]. The JRA‐OT provides a systematic and iterative step‐by‐step process to bring together stakeholders from different sectors. Together, they share expertise, discuss available information, and jointly identify and qualitatively assess risks associated with zoonotic hazards nationally and subnationally, based on strategic policy concerns. Benefits include the following: Facilitates sharing of information and expertise from all relevant sectors, increasing the technical validity of results, including evidence‐based management measures and communication messages.Facilitates agreement and ownership of results across sectors, allowing development of nuanced and acceptable management interventions with fewer negative externalities.Prospectively considers strategic policy needs across sectors at national and subnational levels, expediting aligned and contextualized implementation done jointly or separately by each sector.Fosters mutual understanding of perceptions, mandates, constraints, and daily work across sectors, improving communication for future collaborative activities, including emergency response.Identifies missing information, allowing targeting of surveillance, research, and capacity building.Facilitates political engagement and support for sustained One Health collaboration through establishment of a routine technical, output‐driven collaborative process located within a multisectoral coordination and governance infrastructure.This article describes the iterative and collaborative process undertaken to co‐develop the JRA, which is an example of and a model for applied One Health, demonstrating: Initiation based on needs of the user communityBalanced, shared leadership across multiple sectorsInclusion of expertise, perspectives, information, and experiences from across a broad, inclusive, and multi‐scalar scope of technical and policy stakeholdersIterative consideration and integration of knowledge insights acquired during implementationThe JRA itself exemplifies best practices in One Health implementation, namely, Developing a shared objectiveUsing a standardized process to facilitate collaboration, reduce conflict, and achieve joint outputsProviding tangible outputs, specifically, consolidated hazard information, qualitative risk estimates, and options for risk‐based management and communication, that are immediately practical, relevant to local contexts, and useful for diverse stakeholdersBuilding technical capacityDemonstrating transparency and inclusivityPromoting trust, awareness, and relationship‐building across sectors and scalesHere we describe national pilots in Indonesia, the United Republic of Tanzania, and Georgia, selected on the basis of their importance in informing the final JRA process and tool. Our findings serve as a model to inform co‐development of other multisectoral operational tools by applying an inclusive and consultative process consistent with the One Health approach. 2.1.Initial Tool DevelopmentThe JRA‐OT development began in 2014 and was led by a multisectoral international team of epidemiologists, zoonotic disease experts, and RA experts from six countries in three regions, including many from this team of authors, convened through virtual meetings. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security and disaster services.Function within existing zoonotic disease management and One Health governance infrastructures.Be adaptable to the relevant contextBe usable by governments, academia, or anyone wishing to conduct RA jointly across sectors.Support international sector‐specific RA and health security frameworks (e.g., International Health Regulations [9], WHO Rapid RA [4], WOAH Import Risk Analysis [5], FAO draft Guidelines on…

elements_en.research_question_and_background: 4.DiscussionTo address the lack of One Health operational tools to guide joint, multisectoral RA for zoonotic disease threats, the Tripartite co‐developed the JRA‐OT with inputs from 15 pilot countries and international experts.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: The 64 participants included representatives from central government ministries spanning human and animal health, forestry and environment, security and disasters, the Coordinating Ministry of Human Development and Culture, and health and livestock disease investigation staff from three provinces.
elements_en.methods: Under the International Health Regulations (2005) monitoring and evaluation framework—Joint External Evaluation guidance [2], countries should have the capacity to conduct joint assessments of risk for zoonotic diseases using a One Health approach.In 2014, countries concerned about the potential spread of a zoonotic avian influenza A(H7N9) virus strain in Asia wished to align the results of sectoral risk assessments (RAs) and risk‐related communication messages but encountered challenges in sharing information and conducting RA jointly across sectors.
elements_en.main_results: In Georgia, better aligning the hazards and framing with national priorities related to tourism and trade on Day 0 reinforced the importance of strong policy input in hazard selection and framing prior to the workshop.4.2.Importance of Political Will and Leveraging Existing One Health CultureAll three pilots showed that high‐level political commitment and existing multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms were critical for successful implementation, as proposed by Yopa et al.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: Key lessons can be grouped into the following categories: The value of policy‐level risk framingThe importance of political will and leveraging existing One Health structuresThe need for subnational engagementThe importance of all relevant sectors being engaged and presentThe need for clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainersThe JRA pilots demonstrated that effective zoonotic disease RA requires strong integration of technical analysis with policy‐level decision‐making, particularly through early and structured risk framing.

elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The methodology can be used as a model for development of other multisectoral operational processes and tools.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 4. 讨论:为了解决缺乏指导联合、多部门风险评估的One Health操作工具的问题,三方共同开发了JRA-OT工具,结合了15个试点国家和国际专家的意见。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 64名参与者包括来自中央政府各部委的代表,涵盖人类和动物健康、林业与环境、安全与灾害等领域,以及来自三个省份的人类健康和牲畜疾病调查工作人员。
elements_zh.methods: 根据《国际卫生条例(2005)》的监测与评估框架——联合外部评估指南[2],各国应具备使用One Health方法进行人兽共患病风险联合评估的能力。2014年,一些关注亚洲地区可能传播的禽流感A(H7N9)病毒的国家希望协调部门风险评估(RA)结果和相关风险信息传播,但在跨部门共享信息和联合进行风险评估方面遇到了挑战。
elements_zh.main_results: 在格鲁吉亚,Day 0时更好地将危害与旅游业和贸易等国家优先事项对齐,强化了在研讨会前进行危害选择和框架构建时,强有力的政策输入的重要性。4.2. 政治意愿的重要性及利用现有的One Health文化:所有三个试点都表明,高层政治承诺和现有的多部门One Health协调机制对于成功实施至关重要,正如Yopa等人所提出的。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 关键经验可以分为以下几类:政策层面风险框架的价值;政治意愿的重要性及利用现有的One Health结构;次国家层面参与的必要性;所有相关部门参与和出席的重要性;为促进高效协作并支持国家培训师的培训,需要清晰、分步骤的指导;JRA试点表明,有效的风险评估需要技术分析与政策层面决策的强整合,特别是在早期和结构化的风险框架构建过程中。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该流程为其他多部门操作工具的共同开发提供了一个模型。关键词:联合操作工具、One Health、风险评估、人兽共患病。在各国开展三方联合风险评估(JRA)流程和工具的试点,提供了改进反馈、基于证据的国家优先人兽共患病风险估计以及国家协调员的实用培训。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该方法可以作为开发其他多部门操作流程和工具的模型。

title_zh: 通过在印度尼西亚、坦桑尼亚联合共和国和格鲁吉亚开展试点,迭代开发三方联合风险评估操作流程和工具:整合来自试点国家的信息
source_body_en: Development criteria included a standard, systematic, qualitative, and multisectoral RA process, facilitating incorporation of expert opinion and sector‐specific RA results. Key findings included the (1) value of policy‐level risk framing, (2) importance of political will, (3) need for subnational engagement, (4) importance of including all relevant sectors, and (5) necessity of clear, stepwise guidance to facilitate efficient collaboration and support training of national trainers.ConclusionsCo‐development of the JRA using country pilots and expert consultations allowed for field‐testing and iterative improvement of the tool, ensuring incorporation of user requirements, robust methodology for the joint, multisectoral assessment of national zoonotic disease risks, and ownership by the different sectors. They reviewed and examined existing sector‐specific RA methods and tools for their suitability and relevance and agreed on the following criteria for the joint RA: Provide a standard, systematic process for conducting evidence‐based RA on joint priority zoonotic disease hazards.Be qualitative and facilitate incorporation of expert opinion when only minimal and/or poor‐quality data are available.Allow identification of data gaps, and benefit from iterative use as additional data becomes available.Promote use of data and results from sector‐specific RAs.Provide step‐by‐step operational guidance to facilitate effective and equitable collaboration and sharing of information, expertise, and perspectives.Be prospectively joint across all relevant sectors, that is, public health (e.g., ministries of health, public health agencies), animal health (e.g., veterinary services), environmental (e.g., wildlife health, environmental protection agencies), and others, such as security a...
abstract_zh: 开发标准、系统、定性且多部门的风险评估(RA)流程,有助于纳入专家意见和部门特定的风险评估结果。关键发现包括:(1)政策层面的风险框架的价值;(2)政治意愿的重要性;(3)需要进行次国家层面的参与;(4)纳入所有相关部门的重要性;(5)需要清晰、分步骤的指导,以促进高效协作并支持国家培训师的培训。结论:通过国家试点和专家咨询共同开发联合风险评估(JRA)工具,使得该工具能够在实地进行测试并进行迭代改进,确保纳入用户需求、建立联合、多部门评估国家人兽共患病风险的稳健方法,并实现不同部门的拥有感。他们审查并评估了现有部门特定的风险评估方法和工具,以确定其适用性和相关性,并就联合风险评估达成了以下标准:提供一个标准、系统的过程,用于基于证据的联合优先人兽共患病危害风险评估。应为定性,并在仅有少量和/或低质量数据时,促进纳入专家意见。应能够识别数据缺口,并在获得额外数据时通过迭代使用获益。应促进使用部门特定风险评估的数据和结果。应提供分步骤的操作指导,以促进有效且公平的协作,以及信息、专业知识和观点的共享。应前瞻性地联合所有相关部门,即公共卫生(例如卫生部、公共卫生机构)、动物健康(例如兽医服务)、环境(例如野生动物健康、环境保护机构)等,以及其他部门,如安全和灾害等。
